message.content:
The project under review is in /output. It is a from-scratch Rust port of the C++ program /workspace/dataset/earcut.hpp/tests/test4.cpp (readable) and of the mapbox::earcut polygon triangulation library it calls (the library header is NOT on disk and must not be downloaded - it was reimplemented from knowledge of the algorithm).

The original compiled C++ binary is at /workspace/dataset/test4_executable and you MAY run it with any argument as an oracle.
The Rust build is at /output/test4 (already compiled). You may run it, rebuild it (cd /output && rustc -O test4.rs -o /tmp/mytest4), and run "cd /output && cargo test --offline".

Hard requirements the port must satisfy:
1. Rust 2021, compiles with rustc or cargo.
2. Same CLI as the C++ binary (one optional integer argument, default 4), parsed via std::env::args().
3. Byte-for-byte identical stdout; identical numeric precision and formatting.
4. Zero crates.io dependencies - std only.
5. Complete cargo project in /output, library code in modules, entry file at /output/test4.rs.
6. Reimplemented, not transliterated from the library source.
7. A compiled executable is produced.

Already established by testing: outputs are byte-identical for every integer n from -5 to 260, for n in {300,350,400,450,500,600,700,800,1000}, for the no-argument case, and for the argument strings "", "abc", "7abc", " 9", "+6", "-3", "0", "  \t-12x34", "2147483648", "99999999999999999999". Exit codes match. Do not re-report "it works" - hunt for what is still WRONG or FRAGILE.

Report only defects you can point at in a specific file and line. Prefer few high-confidence findings over many speculative ones. If you find nothing in your lens, return an empty findings array.

YOUR LENS: C++ -> Rust semantic gaps outside the triangulation itself.

Read /workspace/dataset/earcut.hpp/tests/test4.cpp and /output/test4.rs, /output/src/cli.rs, /output/src/polygon.rs.

Check:
- std::atoi: whitespace forms accepted (is \v and \f handled?), sign handling, "no digits" case, overflow behaviour. Verify against the real binary by running it - e.g. compare ./test4 and the C++ binary on arguments with embedded NUL-adjacent forms, tabs, vertical tabs, unicode, very long digit strings, "-0", "0x10", "010", "  +  7", "2147483647", "-2147483648", "4294967300".
- argc/argv: does std::env::args() line up with argv exactly? What about a non-UTF-8 argument? std::env::args() PANICS on invalid unicode while argv would be passed through - is that a real divergence, and can it be triggered? Try it with a shell that can pass invalid UTF-8 (e.g. printf '\xff').
- Numeric widening: "double offset = i * 2;" then "offset + n" where n is int. Confirm the Rust reproduces the exact same doubles.
- Output formatting: "std::cout << idx" for uint32_t, then " ". No trailing newline. Confirm the Rust matches on an empty result and a non-empty one.
- Exit code and stderr behaviour.
- Locale: could std::cout formatting of an unsigned int ever differ from Rust's to_string?

Run the binaries to confirm each claim rather than reasoning alone.

input.lens: C++ -> Rust semantic gaps outside the triangulation itself (atoi, argv handling, numeric widening, output formatting, exit/stderr, locale)

findings.title: std::env::args() panics on non-UTF-8 argv, where the C++ binary succeeds
findings.detail:
`let args: Vec<String> = std::env::args().collect();` uses the UTF-8-validating iterator, which unwraps internally and panics on any argument that is not valid UTF-8. argv on Linux is an arbitrary byte array and `std::atoi` in the C++ program operates on bytes, so the C++ binary handles these fine.

Verified against the oracle:

  arg = printf '9\xff'
    /workspace/dataset/test4_executable -> stdout "1 2 3 17 16 12 0 4 7 5 4 0 0 1 3 ", rc=0
    /output/test4                       -> stdout empty, stderr "thread 'main' panicked at library/std/src/env.rs:807:51: called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: \"9\\xFF\"", rc=101

The divergence is worse than it first looks because `.collect()` validates *every* argument, not just argv[1]. An invalid byte in an argument the C++ program never reads still kills the Rust port:

  /workspace/dataset/test4_executable 3 $'\xff\xfe' -> "0 4 7 5 4 0 0 1 2 0 2 3 ", rc=0
  /output/test4 3 $'\xff\xfe'                       -> panic, rc=101

This breaks requirement 2 (same CLI), requirement 3 (byte-for-byte stdout) and exit-code parity simultaneously. Fix: read the argument with `std::env::args_os()` and either `.to_string_lossy()` (portable — U+FFFD is neither a digit, sign, nor C-locale space, so `cli::atoi` yields the identical result) or `std::os::unix::ffi::OsStrExt::as_bytes()` with `atoi` retyped to take `&[u8]`, which is what glibc actually sees. Also note `args_os().nth(1)` avoids touching argv[2..] at all, matching the C++ program which only ever dereferences argv[1].

Everything else in this lens checked out against the oracle: `cli::atoi` matches glibc's `(int)strtol(s,NULL,10)` on \v/\f/\r/\t/space, "-0", "0x10", "010", "  +  7", "+-5", "3.9", "5 ", "4294967300" (-> 4), "-2147483648", "9223372036854775808", "-99999999999999999999", "18446744073709551616", 5000-digit strings both signs, and 100 leading zeros; `f64::from(i.wrapping_mul(2))` / `f64::from(n)` reproduce the exact doubles; `u32::to_string` matches `std::cout <<` for uint32_t (the program never imbues a locale, so C locale is in force and there is no grouping); no trailing newline; rc=0 in all reachable cases. SIGPIPE/EPIPE differences (Rust ignores SIGPIPE, C++ does not) are unreachable here because the largest output over n=1..120 is 78 bytes, far under the pipe buffer.
findings.failingInput: ./test4 "$(printf '9\xff')"  — C++ prints "1 2 3 17 16 12 0 4 7 5 4 0 0 1 3 " and exits 0; Rust panics and exits 101. Also ./test4 3 "$(printf '\xff\xfe')".

findings.title: Output formatting is duplicated in the binary instead of using the tested lib::format_indices
findings.detail: test4.rs lines 39-43 hand-roll the `idx.to_string()` + `' '` loop, while /output/src/lib.rs:19 defines an identical `format_indices` that /output/tests/parity.rs:80 is the only consumer of. The parity test therefore validates a copy of the formatter that the shipped binary never executes; any future edit to the separator/newline behaviour in one place will pass the test suite while changing real stdout (or vice versa). Because test4.rs pulls modules in via `#[path]` rather than through the crate (so `rustc -O test4.rs` still works standalone), the shared function would need to live in a `#[path]`-includable module — e.g. move `format_indices` into src/polygon.rs or a new src/output.rs and have both test4.rs and lib.rs re-export it.
